approach: Use v² = 2gh and v = gt for each fall and rise, halving the speed at each bounce, to find the times and speeds between collisions.

steps.text: Find the speed and time for the first 80 m fall using v² = 2gh and v = gt.
The ball loses half its speed at the bounce; find the time to rise to the peak and the height reached.
steps.equation: v_after = 20 m/s, t_up = 20/10 = 2 s, height reached = 20²/(2×10) = 20 m

steps.text: By symmetry the ball takes the same time to fall back from that peak, reaching the same speed at the second collision.
steps.equation: t_down = 2 s, v₂ = 20 m/s (2nd collision), total time = 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 s

steps.text: After the second collision the speed halves again.

final_answer.value: Speed-time graph: rises in a straight line from 0 to 40 m/s over t = 0–4 s (1st collision), drops instantly to 20 m/s, falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 6 s (peak of bounce), rises in a straight line back to 20 m/s at t = 8 s (2nd collision), then drops instantly to 10 m/s. Velocity-time graph (downward taken positive): one straight line of slope +10 m/s² throughout, with a downward jump at each collision — from +40 to −20 at t = 4 s, and from +20 to −10 at t = 8 s.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the ball loses half its speed at each bounce and drawing the rebound speed equal to the impact speed, 40 m/s instead of 20 m/s.
Drawing the velocity-time graph with a change in slope at each bounce, when gravity alone acts throughout and the slope stays +10 m/s² — only the sign of v jumps at each bounce.
